newsitem.title: INDIA: PRESS DIGEST - Indian newspapers - February 21.
newsitem.headline: PRESS DIGEST - Indian newspapers - February 21.

text.p: Following is a summary of major Indian business and political stories in leading newspapers prepared for REUTERS by Business News and Information Services Pvt Ltd, New Delhi Tel:3324842, 3351006, 3761233 Fax:+91-11-3351006 Internet: biznis@giasbm01.vsnl.net.in
Reuters has not verified these stories and does not vouch for their accuracy.
TOP STORIES
The Times Of India
DELETION IN PRESIDENT'S ADDRESS SPARKS ROW

Deletion of a sentence from the text of the president's address to the joint session of parliament kicked up a controversy. The address, which marks the opening of the budget session, reflects the policies and programmes of the government. The sentence, which held previous governments responsible for their failure to meet the challenges facing the country, was deleted under pressure from the Congress. Though the party denied having anything to do with it, the Congress took exception to it after seeing the text before it was delivered. The decision to delete the sentence at the last minute was taken by the president, vice-president and prime minister, shortly before they entered parliamen
The Economic Times
DIVESTMENT IN GAIL, ITDC, MODERN FOOD MOOTED

The government's disinvestment panel recommended a 25 percent divestment in Gas Authority (GAIL) and an outright sale of government equity in Modern Food. The panel, in its first set of recommendations, also mooted a de-merger of Indian Tourism Development Corporation hotels in small towns, spinning them into separate firms and selling them, subject to an overall divestment ceiling of 74 percent. It identified 20 state-owned firms as core sector companies where divestment of up to 49 percent should be allowed. Similarly, 15 non-core outfits were picked, with a divestment level of upto 74 percent.
PANEL TO REVIEW TATA AIRPORT PROJECT

A panel was set up to review the Tata-Raytheon proposal for an airport project. The panel would study the merits and demerits of a build-operate-transfer (BOT) and build-operate-own (BOO) model. The civil aviation minister, who previously insisted on a BOT format for the project, said both models should be considered and studied. The global tenders floated for the project were, however, on a BOO arrangement.
IMMEDIATE SUSPENSION OF UREA SALES ORDERED

The government ordered an immediate suspension of all sales by urea makers and importers in a bid to prevent inflation of its fertiliser subsidy bill. All state governments were being asked to physically ensure sellers sold urea at the old prices and did not indulge in hoarding. The move followed the recent decision to hike urea prices by 10 percent, without indicating the date from when these prices would be effective. The resultant confusion in the market and fear of ante-dated sales, while still claiming a higher subsidy on the old rates, compelled the government to take this step, sources said.
FINANCIAL INSTITUTIONS WANT MORE AUTONOMY

Smarting under the tight control exercised over them by the Finance Ministry, financial institutions (FIs) sought the help of members of parliament (MPs) to secure more autonomy. They complained to the members of the parliamentary panel studying the functioning of FIs, of interference by the ministry in their day to day functioning. Officials of the Life Insurance Corporation and the Unit Trust of India said the lack of autonomy prevented them from deploying surplus funds profitably.
PASSENGER CARS RECORD NEGATIVE GROWTH RATE

The year-on-year growth rates in passenger cars witnessed volatile trends in the current fiscal even as the growth rate in November showed a negative downtrend. As against a 30-40 percent growth rate witnessed in the first quarter of 1996/97 (April-March), rates declined to 67 percent in September 1996 only to bounce back to 35-40 percent in October. But growth in sales fell again in November, CMIE said. Cumulative production of passenger cars in the first nine months of 1996/97, at 0.29 million was 18.5 percent higher than the 0.25 million produced in the corresponding period of 1995/96, it said in a report.
Financial Express
APEX BANK RELAXES CAPITAL ADEQUACY NORMS

The Reserve Bank of India relaxed capital adequacy norms for commercial banks. For the first time, it allowed all banks to net off credit balances in current or other accounts not specially earmarked -- and free from any lien -- to calculate the aggregate of funded and non-funded exposure of a corporate borrower. Previously, banks were allowed to work out risk adjusted values of assets and off-balance sheet items by netting off only cash margins or deposits which act as collaterals for advances. In respect of bad and doubtful debts provisions were also allowed to be netted off for calculating the exposure limit.
LOBBYING ON AGAINST SRF TAKEOVER

The takeover of SRF Finance by GE Capital came under fire at the Foreign Investment Promotion Board, with several Indian groups lobbying to have the takeover stalled. GE was yet to get the necessary approvals to formalise the takeover through its Mauritius outfit. The principal lobby attacking the merger included some of the bidders who lost out to GE despite having made better offers. They were joined by the anti-multinational lobby working through industry bodies.
Business Standard
SPECIAL CUSTOMS DUTY MAY GO UP

The two percent customs duty imposed by the finance minister in his first budget presented in July 1996 would not only be continued in 1997/98 (April-March), but may be raised to five percent. Imperatives of bringing down the fiscal deficit had forced the minister to impose the levy, which was expected to have fetched 16 billion rupees. The duty was levied on all imports except gold and silver brought in as passenger baggage and all items with a nil rate of duty. The Finance Ministry had argued in favour of a further hike in the duty, if the goals of fiscal deficit reduction as well as a general reduction in customs duty on a wide range of items was to be achieved in 1997/98.
REFERENCE TO OPENING UP INSURANCE ANGERS LEFT

The opening up of the insurance sector to foreign investment found a mention in the president's address to both houses of parliament. This was resented by the Marxist Communist Party (CPM), one of the constituents of the ruling coalition. The CPM declared it would oppose the move in the ongoing budget session. The party said it found several references in the presidential speech to be objectionable and decided to seek clarifications from the government. The CPM had also raised objections on some of the provisions in the broadcasting bill.
TATA SONS TO RAISE STAKE IN GROUP FIRMS

Tata Sons decided to hike its stake in major group companies. The plan was aimed to ensure Tata Sons had a meaningful holding in the companies it managed, a company spokesman said. He said the strategy was unconnected with the takeover code. Sources said the primary objective was to raise Tata Sons' stake in group companies to 26 percent. They said the strategy stemmed from the threat Tata Sons perceived once the takeover code was notified. Tata holdings in most of the major group firms are way below the safety mark.
FINANCE FIRMS TO CHALLENGE ORDINANCE

Non-banking finance companies (NBFCs) proposed challenging in court provisions of the recent central bank (RBI) amendment ordinance 1997. While none of the NBFcs opposed the imposition of sinking fund and other regulations, the point of contention was the RBI's banning of unincorporated bodies from accepting deposits. The Hire Purchase Association said the ordinance did not distinguish between genuine NBFCs and fly-by-night operators.
The Observer
BAT PROPOSAL STILL ON HOLD

British multinational BAT's proposed wholly-owned subsidiary was proving to be another thorny issue for the government. BAT's proposal for setting up a 100 percent holding company, was cleared by the government in January this year. However, it was understood have been to be put on hold by the industry minister. The decision was influenced by the finance minister, who considered the proposal to be sensitive, in the light of the ITC-BAT tangle. With the issue poised delicately, the industry minister was advised by his finance counterpart, to keep the government off the matter at this point.
RAIL FREIGHT MAY GO UP BY 15-20 PCT

A 15 to 20 percent hike in freight charges and 10 percent increase in upper class passenger fares was being contemplated in the railway budget. Sources said the sharp increase was inevitable considering the railway minister's commitment not to do away with social obligations, expansion to backward and strategically important areas and the additional outlay imposed on account of the Pay Panel recommendations and other measures. The ministry also planned a five percent increase on the second class fares as well as introduction of a dual tariff structure for urban commuters, the sources said.
PHILIPS INDIA PROFIT DIPS 65 PCT

The net profit of 14.85 billion rupee Philips India went down 64.8 percent in the year ended December 1996. In the year ended 1995 the profit was 2.29 billion rupees which dwindled to 807 million rupees in the latest year. The decline in profit was against a two percent decline in turnover from 15.2 billion rupees in end 1995 to 14.85 billion rupees this year. The Philips India chairman attributed the decline in the net profit to higher interest burden and higher depreciation charges.
CEMENT, POWER UNITS TO BE HIT

The government's decision on deregulating D-grade coal is likely to affect the cement and power industries, with the prospect of a steep hike in prices. Most of the cement, fertilizer and power companies, which have modern technology, were the bulk consumers of this category presently. Coal India (CIL) sources said, the run of mine (RoM) price of the D-grade coal was likely to increase by 18-20 percent at least. The cement and power industries were reported to have made a representation to the government against any further hike in the prices, and demanded a cut in the import duty on coal which was now 20 percent.
BUDGET MAY HIT AUTO INDUSTRY

The budget proposals for 1997/98 (April-March) were likely to cheer capital goods, textiles, polymers and iron and steel firms. It may, however, disappoint auto manufacturers while some industries such as cement, fertilisers and aluminium were unlikely to witness major developments. These observations were made by ICICI Securities and Finance Company (I-Sec), a JP Morgan affiliate, in its pre-budget reports. I-Sec forecast higher excise for diesel and luxury cars, a marginal reduction in customs for capital goods and cuts in excise duty for steel products.
